items.content:
Quick run-down to check if @MeTerminator666 is right: 

This is part of Xiaomi's AI通话防护 ( AI Guard anti fraud ) service. It bypasses user notification and has no consent dialogue. 

We got the apk samples and the system and found the use of 'mediaProjection', leading to the screen recording feature.

It writes an 3sec H264 clip at 1Mbps and stores it in the phone's cache before sending it on to, it gives a 2sec wait time before trying again. As stated it is encoded in base64 and does it every 5 seconds during a monitored called. It tries to upload them until it gets a negative or a positive back from the detection engine. 

This is where the detection engine lives: "const-string v1, 'https://t.co/kg1sVa2jWm' "

If positive the user gets an alert that is reoccurring until he either hangs up or marks the alert as 'false positive'. The choices are recorded too. 
Further it transcribes the calls when the video is not available via its built in ASR engine it seems. This is also send encrypted to the above detection engine address. We could not find out if all calls are recorded/transcribed or only flagged ones ( or what constitutes the flagging ). 

All the data is encrypted via Xiaomi's on PCC SDK. 

That said though, the AI Guard feature can be switched off. So, it is not always operational it seems.

items.content:
RT @GrahamHelton3: Long post regarding "Black October" as someone who gets paid to hack into companies:

A lot of people are just starting to pay attention to cybersecurity, and that is a wonderful thing, but we should be honest about what is new versus what is only now being discovered by those who have just started paying attention.

I took a biology class in high school where we had a module on germs. The teacher gave everyone a cotton swab and petri dish to hunt down and swab 1 disgusting place and 1 clean place. After a weekend, we returned amazed that every petri dish had fuzzy little friends growing, even the ones from the "clean" places.

I keep thinking about those petri dishes when I hear people talk about "Black October", a term being used to describe all the vulnerabilities reported this month (October 2026). For the first time, a lot of people outside of security are seeing what happens when you look closely at software. Finding germs on a surface is easy when you have a swab and a petri dish, but figuring out if they can make you sick is quite hard. The same goes for software. AI can help find a lot of bugs, but finding a bug is not the same as:

Understanding the conditions required to exploit it
Showing which real systems meet those conditions.
Demonstrating that it can be exploited in those systems.
Showing that other defenses don't stop the attack.
Demonstrating that the attack gives someone access or capabilities they didn't already have.

Last week when the whole world started trying to get a reliable exploit for php2shell, it was fascinating to see the number of very smart people claim they had a working exploit, only to find out that their exploit relied on a vulnerable lab setup. If you don't have a background in this type of work, it is very easy to overlook this and make grandiose and incorrect claims about security.

There is another reason the focus on newly discovered bugs feels wrong to me. Finding a vulnerability in code is only one way to break into a company. This is surprising to people, but in my own red team work I rarely need to rely on vulnerabilities. More often than not, I'm using features that work exactly as designed. Phishing doesn't require a zero-day vulnerability in email infrastructure, email is supposed to deliver messages. A malicious software package doesn't require a zero-day vulnerability, the package manager is supposed to install software.

This is not new or novel in any way. The security industry knows this. We even have a fancy lexicon for classifying attack techniques (which I have contributed to) called MITRE ATT&CK. The majority of those techniques don't require a software vulnerability.

The hard part of offensive security has always been showing that an attacker can exploit a bug against a real system, get past the defenses in place, and gain information or a capability they couldn't otherwise. Without doing that work or understanding the processes in place for properly finding, validating, and disclosing issues, it's easy to mistake an interesting bug for a fully exploitable vulnerability. When that claim is made publicly, it spreads very fast. News organizations request for comment, Incident response teams are paged, maintainers have to respond, and offensive security teams start digging. If that claim turns out to be overblown or incorrect, you've wasted a massive amount of resources and rebuilding that trust will be difficult.

items.content:
It was great to speak with so many of the smartest vulnerability researchers in the world this week at OffensiveCon Tokyo.

One key takeaway from speaking to colleagues and contemporaries in the government contracting side of the industry: The AI agent pipelines, no matter how they’re laid out, which models one uses, or how much they spend on tokens in the process, are all converging on the same bugs. But in A/B tests, where we have some of our best human researchers (*I mean dudes that make and have made for years $4M/year on account of how many A-grade exploits they surface) pull apart the latest versions of iOS/Android/Chrome or whatever, in the way that they used to do before AI, these hugely talented human researchers find bugs that are utterly unique, and far higher quality, and that none of the models are finding. Even when those models/agents are armed with the same data and tools (decompilers, debuggers, etc). 

Also, the human researcher only gets paid the lion’s share of their compensation at such a point as you are sure that you are able to actually generate revenue from their discoveries. The precise details of this split between salary and bonus can vary, of course. 

Whereas with the AI agents, it’s very easy to find one’s self having spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on tokens, only to have those tokens generate the same bugs that the same model (or other models distilled from that model) already generated for like 15 other people around the world; half of whom have no access to responsible government buyers for said discoveries and so will thus be reporting back to the vendor in exchange for a $5K bounty.

items.content:
If you asked GPT-4 a chemistry problem, it would either give you the correct solution from its memory, or it would “hallucinate” and give you the wrong answer. But it would give you an answer. And it would do so without tool-calls, internet search, etc. 

Depending on the topic, it would give the wrong answer a high percentage of the time. 

So naturally, the labs put a premium on giving the models the ability to search the web, access tools like scripts and calculators, spawn sub-agents, etc. 

The frontier labs all but gave up on trying to get the models to memorize and recite facts and data correctly. Altman & co would explain “LLMs are not databases and they’re really bad at being databases. If you ask it who won the World Series in 1929, you’re using it wrong. It’s a substrate to reason over text.”

And so the era of tool calls started. Some companies like Perplexity (currently somehow valued at $20B+) got an early start on this, delivering basic SerpAPI+LLM as a service with some basic caching to speed it up. 

Now that it’s been 2 years since the foundation labs seemingly gave up on training facts into the weights of the models such that the models can recite them quickly and correctly, it seems that this capability is an incredibly auspicious gap that poses a major inconvenience.  

Earlier today, I randomly wondered to myself “I wonder if the placebo effect is strong enough such that in studies, people given saline instead of insulin were able to somehow “think” their blood sugar down?”

So I asked ChatGPT, and I also texted a friend of mine who is a very accomplished pharmaceutical researcher. My friend texted me back almost instantly and even included a reference, and ChatGPT went searching all over the internet for 10 minutes to give me the same answer. 

It would be much preferred if the model could just recall facts accurately, the way that you and I and my pharmaceutical researcher friend can.

RT @MeTerminator666: 【奉劝大家不要用国产机翻墙，不要在国产机上安卓境外 APP】
我某些朋友用的国产安卓手机，前不久被当地公安打电话，要求卸载 X 和 Telegram，因为我其中一个朋友的小米 14 已经 root 了，我觉得因为梯子配置不当导致的 DNS 泄露，或者别的原因，可能性不大，我就重点排查手机上会上报应用列表的应用

经排查，我朋友的小米 14，HyperOS 3，其中的“系统安全组件”和“SystemHelper”，会分别把应用列表上报给小米反诈引擎（fraud-detection.engine.miui[.]com/hyperos/fraud/app/report和flash.sec.miui[.]com/detect/app）和联通的某个网址（dm.wo[.]com[.]cn:18080/register）

SystemHelper 会默认统计过去 24 小时内有使用记录的应用，枚举已安装应用，关联使用统计和流量，跳过包名以 com[.]android 开头的条目。载荷的序列化实现还包含 IMEI、IMSI、ICCID 等字段，因此具备将应用情况与设备/SIM 标识关联上报的能力。

系统安全组件会上报第三方应用清单、包名、版本、签名摘要、名称，另有扫描结果和仿冒应用上报；有电话/QQ/微信语音反诈、屏幕视频采集、转写文本和视频片段云检测，以及用户反馈上传原始音频的实现

关于系统安全组件的录屏采集功能，分辨率 720 × 1280，24 fps，固定竖屏尺寸。相关的流程如下：
取得系统录屏对象
 → 录制约 3 秒屏幕画面到私有缓存文件
 → 读取整段 MP4，转为 Base64
 → 加密后上传小米云端
 → 等待返回“是否风险”
     ├─ 未命中：删除临时片段，延时 2 秒后继续录制，重复上述行为
     └─ 命中：保留一份片段供反馈，显示警告并停止服务

这些应用，SystemHelper 貌似是和 SIM 卡激活相关的，系统安全组件貌似是和反诈相关的，但是都具有高度的数据上报属性。没有 root 的机器，这些组件是无法卸载或者提取的，并且我也暂未分析这两个 APP 卸载之后，会不会自己下载回来。

综上，还是建议大家，海外产业用外版 iPhone，尽量不要碰国行安卓，要用安卓机，也是刷 ASOP 使用。

逆向由 GPT 完成，如有错误，敬请指正。

items.content:
RT @0x_exit: I can’t stop thinking about this… before hackers stole $6.4 billion from Binance, they spent days rehearsing the attack in public. The test transactions on Ethereum were worth only a few dollars. Nobody stopped them.

Bloomberg reconstructed what happened. Once the code worked, the hackers launched the real attack across multiple blockchains.

Then I reached the detail that doesn’t feel real. Some of the compromised wallets kept receiving fresh funds from Binance while the hackers were draining them. The attackers emptied a wallet, Binance refilled it, and they emptied it again. For a period of time, the exchange was effectively feeding new money into its own robbery.

Binance co-founder Yi He was at home in Abu Dhabi. She reportedly discovered the breach while scrolling X before bed. Imagine opening Twitter and learning that billions of dollars are disappearing from your own exchange.

Within minutes, Binance assembled a 100 person crisis team. The FBI, the U.S. Secret Service and blockchain analysts around the world joined the response. Meanwhile, some employees were reportedly already worried about losing their annual bonuses.

But the most disturbing detail came later. According to the investigation, the hackers used valid permissions to execute the transfers. To the blockchain, everything looked authorized. There was no transaction labeled “hack” just legitimate-looking operations moving billions out of wallets the system still trusted.

The $6.4 billion heist didn’t begin when billions started moving. It began days earlier with transactions worth a few dollars, too small for anyone to care about.

By the time it looked dangerous, the blockchain was still saying: authorized.
